lead: Coarse solids that let liquid drain through them are leached without stirring: solvent percolates through a stationary bed, or the solid is carried slowly against the solvent in a moving bed, or several stationary beds are connected so that the liquor passes through them in turn and the positions are switched as each bed is exhausted, which is the Shanks system. All three aim at counter-current contact, because the leanest solid then meets the cleanest solvent and the product liquor leaves strong. Their stage calculations use the inert-solid basis of leaching, with the first stage treated separately when the feed brings dry solute.
prereq: You need Leaching: principles, equipment and stage calculations (inert basis, retained solution L = rI, ideal stage).

blocks.text: In percolation the crushed or sliced solid is loaded into a tank with a perforated false bottom. Solvent is sprayed or flooded on top, trickles or flows down through the voids and is drawn off below. Solute near the particle surface comes out first, so the first runnings are strong; later runnings are weak because the remaining solute must diffuse from deep in the particles. A bed can be run as repeated flood–soak–drain cycles, each cycle acting roughly as a stage, or with continuous downward flow. The particles must be coarse and uniform enough for even flow; fines cause channelling and slow drainage. Coffee extraction, tea, tanning materials and the old sugar-beet diffusion batteries are percolation processes.

sections.h3: Moving beds and the Shanks system

blocks.text: In a moving-bed extractor the solid is moved through the machine while the solvent moves the other way: baskets on a chain in the Bollman extractor, a rotating ring of cells in the Rotocel, screws in tower and U-tube extractors. The solid leaves where the fresh solvent enters, and the strong liquor (the miscella, in oil extraction) leaves where the fresh solid enters.

The Shanks system gets counter-current contact without moving the solid. A battery of percolation tanks is connected by pipes and valves. Fresh solvent is fed to the tank with the most nearly exhausted solid; the liquor passes in series through the tanks holding progressively fresher solid and leaves as strong liquor from the tank just charged with fresh solid. When the oldest tank is spent it is cut out, emptied and refilled with fresh solid, and the valves are changed so that this refilled tank becomes the last one the liquor passes through. Fresh solvent then goes to the tank that was second oldest. The inlet and outlet positions advance one tank per cycle round the battery, so over time the solid appears to move against the liquor. The same principle is used in continuous counter-current decantation with thickeners.

Number the stages from the solid feed end: stage 1 takes the fresh solid and delivers the strong overflow V<sub>1</sub>; stage N takes the fresh solvent W and delivers the spent underflow. Assume ideal stages and constant underflow: every underflow carries L = rB kg of solution with B kg/h of inert. For a dry feed carrying A kg/h of solute, an overall solution balance gives V<sub>1</sub> = W + A − L. In stages 2 to N the overflow rate is constant and equal to W, so in that section the washing factor is E = W/L.
y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub> = (E − 1)/(E<sup>N</sup> − 1),  E = W/L ≠ 1;    A = V<sub>1</sub>y<sub>1</sub> + L y<sub>N</sub>
blocks.where: y<sub>1</sub> is the solute fraction of the strong overflow (and of the underflow solution leaving stage 1); y<sub>N</sub> that of the solution in the spent underflow; the first relation is the Kremser equation for the N − 1 washing stages 2 to N with pure solvent; the second is the overall solute balance. Solve the two together for y<sub>1</sub> and y<sub>N</sub>. If E = 1, y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub> = 1/N.

blocks.text: For multistage cross-current washing, each stage gets its own fresh solvent Wn and yn = yn−1L/(L + Wn). Counter-current uses the same solvent in every washing stage, so for the same total solvent it loses far less solute and gives a stronger product. When r changes with concentration, the stages are stepped on the N–y diagram with a difference point, exactly as on the extraction triangle. Real stages are fewer than ideal ones: real stages = ideal stages/overall stage efficiency.

examples.question: 1000 kg/h of solid holding 25 mass% soluble solute and 75 mass% inert is leached in a three-stage ideal counter-current battery with 600 kg/h of fresh water. Every underflow retains 0.6 kg of solution per kg of inert. Find the strong-liquor flow and strength, the solute lost and the recovery. How many ideal stages give at least 95 % recovery?
steps: Inert B = 750 kg/h; solute A = 250 kg/h; retained solution L = 0.6 × 750 = 450 kg/h.
Strong overflow V<sub>1</sub> = W + A − L = 600 + 250 − 450 = 400 kg/h. In stages 2 and 3 the overflow is 600 kg/h, so E = 600/450 = 1.333.
Solute balance: 250 = 400 y<sub>1</sub> + 450 × 0.2432 y<sub>1</sub> = 509.5 y<sub>1</sub>, so y<sub>1</sub> = 0.4907 and y<sub>3</sub> = 0.1194.

Stage-by-stage check: y<sub>2</sub> follows from stage 3, 450 y<sub>2</sub> = (450 + 600) y<sub>3</sub>, so y<sub>2</sub> = 0.2785; stage 1: 250 + 600 × 0.2785 = (400 + 450) × 0.4907 gives 417.1 = 417.1.
Solute lost = L y<sub>3</sub> = 450 × 0.1194 = 53.7 kg/h; strong liquor carries 400 × 0.4907 = 196.3 kg/h; recovery 196.3/250 = 78.5 %.
Repeating step 3 and 4 for more stages: N = 4 gives 85.2 %, N = 6 gives 92.5 %, N = 7 gives 94.5 %, N = 8 gives 96.0 %. So 8 ideal stages are needed for 95 %.
examples.answer: Strong liquor 400 kg/h at 49.1 % solute; 53.7 kg/h lost; recovery 78.5 %. Eight ideal stages reach 95 % (96.0 %).

traps: The overflow from stage 1 (400 kg/h) is not the overflow in the washing stages (600 kg/h): the dry feed's solute dissolves only in stage 1. Using E = 400/450 for the whole battery gives 70.4 % instead of 78.5 %.
Stage 1 is not a washing stage; the Kremser relation covers the N − 1 stages from 2 to N.
In the Shanks system the solid does not move; the inlet and outlet of the liquor are switched round the battery.
Strong liquor leaves from the tank (or stage) holding the freshest solid, not from the one receiving fresh solvent.
Solids and liquor flowing the same way (co-current) give little more than one ideal stage however many tanks are used, because the two streams leave together at the same composition.

quiz.q: In a Shanks battery, which tank receives fresh solvent and which delivers strong liquor?
quiz.a: Fresh solvent enters the tank with the most nearly exhausted solid; strong liquor leaves from the tank most recently charged with fresh solid.

quiz.q: Why are the first runnings of a percolation bed stronger than the later ones?
quiz.a: Solute at and near the particle surfaces dissolves and washes out at once; later solute must diffuse from the particle interiors through depleted pores, so the liquor gets weaker.

quiz.q: B = 500 kg/h of inert retains r = 0.8 kg solution per kg inert. Find L.
E = 2 in the washing stages of a 3-stage counter-current battery. Find y<sub>3</sub>/y<sub>1</sub>.
In the worked example, what recovery does a single ideal stage give with the same 600 kg/h of water?
quiz.a: M = 850 kg/h, y = 250/850 = 0.294; overflow 400 kg/h carries 117.6 kg/h, recovery 47.1 %.

quiz.q: Why does counter-current washing beat cross-current washing for the same total solvent?
quiz.a: In counter-current flow the whole solvent flow passes every washing stage and leaves through the strong end, so the solid's last solution is washed by clean solvent while the product picks up solute stage by stage. Cross-current splits the solvent, so each stage gets only a part and every overflow is dilute.

quiz.q: A battery needs 8 ideal stages and the overall stage efficiency is 0.65. How many real stages are installed?

beyond: Not for the exam. Continuous moving-bed extractors (Rotocel, loop and belt types) handle thousands of tonnes of soybean flakes per day, with miscella recycled cell by cell exactly as in a Shanks battery. Sugar-beet plants use continuous counter-current diffusers. Hydrometallurgy uses counter-current decantation trains of thickeners and heap leaching. Search for Rotocel extractor, sugar beet diffuser and counter-current decantation design.
